phy_edx.7.0.summary: Energy is held in stores (kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, nuclear, magnetic and electrostatic) and is transferred between them when a system changes. The energy of a system can be changed through work done by forces, in electrical equipment and in heating, and these transfers can be shown in flow diagrams and Sankey diagrams. In a closed system the total energy never changes: energy is conserved, simply moving from one store to another.

core.p: Spec points 8.1 to 8.4 are about describing **how energy is stored** in a system, how it is **transferred** when the system changes, and the idea that in a **closed system** the **total energy stays the same**. You also need to know the **three ways** the energy of a system can be changed: **work done by forces**, **in electrical equipment** and **in heating**.
bullets: 8.1: describe the changes in the way energy is stored when systems change (five named examples).
8.2: **draw and interpret diagrams** of energy transfers (flow diagrams and **Sankey diagrams**).
8.3: explain that in a **closed system** there is **no net change to the total energy**.
8.4: identify the ways energy can be changed: **work done by forces**, **electrical equipment**, **heating**.
This underpins the rest of Topic 8 (work, GPE, KE, power and efficiency).

core.p: A **system** is the object or group of objects you choose to study. Choosing the system carefully makes energy accounting possible: you track energy going into and out of the stores inside it.
bullets: Example: a ball and the Earth form a system when a ball is thrown upwards.
Example: a kettle, the water in it and the surrounding air.
When a system changes (moves, heats up, stretches), energy is **transferred between stores**.
Energy is never 'used up'; it is moved from one store to another.

callouts.p: An object or group of objects that we choose to consider when describing energy changes.

core.p: Energy is described as being held in **stores**. You must name stores precisely; mark schemes reward the word **store** with the correct type.
bullets: **Kinetic** store: any moving object.
**Gravitational potential** store: an object raised in a gravitational field.
**Elastic potential** store: a stretched, squashed or bent object (spring, catapult).
**Thermal** store: every object; more energy when hotter.
**Chemical** store: fuels, food, batteries.
**Nuclear** store: atomic nuclei, released in fission and fusion.
**Magnetic** store: magnets attracting or repelling.
**Electrostatic** store: charges attracting or repelling.

callouts.t: Light and sound are not stores
callouts.p: Light and sound are ways energy is transferred (by radiation or waves), not stores. Do not write 'sound energy store'.

core.p: Energy moves between stores along **pathways**. The Edexcel spec (8.4) names three ways the energy of a system can be changed.
bullets: **Work done by forces** (mechanically): a force moves an object, e.g. pushing, lifting, friction.
**In electrical equipment** (electrically): an electric current transfers energy, e.g. a battery driving a motor.
**In heating**: energy transferred because of a **temperature difference**, from hotter to cooler.
Energy is also carried by **radiation** (light, infrared) and by **sound waves**, e.g. from a lamp or speaker.
In every case energy leaves one store and enters another.

callouts.p: The energy of a system can be changed through work done by forces, in electrical equipment, and in heating.

core.h: Example 1: object projected upwards (or up a slope)
core.p: When a ball is thrown upwards, it starts fast and low, and ends momentarily still at its highest point.
bullets: At launch the energy is mostly in the **kinetic store** of the ball.
As it rises, the **gravitational force (weight) does work** against its motion, transferring energy from the **kinetic store** to the **gravitational potential store**.
At the top, speed is zero: kinetic store is empty, GPE store is at maximum.
Some energy is transferred to the **thermal store of the surroundings** by air resistance, so it rises slightly less high than with no air.
Rolling up a slope is the same: kinetic store to GPE store, with some to thermal stores by friction.

core.h: Example 2: moving object hitting an obstacle
core.p: When a moving object hits something and stops, its kinetic store empties. The energy goes into other stores through work done by the contact forces.
bullets: Energy is transferred from the **kinetic store** of the object.
Forces at the impact **do work** deforming the object and obstacle.
Energy ends up mostly in the **thermal stores** of the object, obstacle and surroundings (they warm up slightly).
Some is carried away by **sound** waves, which then also warms the surroundings.
If the object bounces (e.g. a ball), some energy is briefly in its **elastic potential store**, then back to kinetic.

core.h: Example 3: object accelerated by a constant force
core.p: When a constant resultant force pushes an object, it speeds up. The force does work on the object.
bullets: The force **does work** on the object, transferring energy to its **kinetic store**.
The energy comes from whatever provides the force, e.g. the **chemical store** of a person's muscles or fuel, or the **elastic store** of a stretched catapult.
If friction acts, some energy goes to the **thermal store** of the surroundings, so the kinetic store gains less.
The larger the force or the further it acts, the more work is done, so the bigger the increase in kinetic store (see W = F x d in 8.5 to 8.7).

core.p: When a car brakes, friction between the brake pads and the discs slows it down. This is a key exam example.
bullets: Energy is transferred from the **kinetic store of the car**.
The pathway is **work done by friction** (forces) between brake pads and discs.
Energy goes to the **thermal store of the brakes**, which get hot, and then to the **thermal store of the surroundings**.
Some energy also goes to the surroundings by sound and by air resistance.
Hybrid and electric cars use **regenerative braking**: some kinetic energy is transferred electrically to the **chemical store** of the battery instead of being wasted.

core.h: Example 5: boiling water in an electric kettle
core.p: An electric kettle is the standard example of energy transferred in electrical equipment and by heating.
bullets: Energy is transferred **electrically** from the mains (from the power station) to the heating element.
The element gets hot; energy is transferred **by heating** to the **thermal store of the water**, raising its temperature.
Some energy is transferred to the **thermal store of the kettle** itself and to the **thermal store of the surroundings** (wasted).
Some energy is carried away as **sound** and by water evaporating as steam.
Useful energy = energy into the thermal store of the water.

core.h: Closed systems and conservation of energy
core.p: The **law of conservation of energy** says energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores. In a **closed system**, nothing enters or leaves, so the total energy cannot change.
bullets: A **closed system** is one where **no energy (or matter) is transferred in or out** of the system.
Energy can move between stores **inside** a closed system.
But the **total energy in the system stays the same**: there is **no net change**.
Example: a ball and the Earth with no air resistance: decrease in KE store = increase in GPE store.
If energy seems to 'disappear', it has gone into a store you did not include (usually thermal stores of the surroundings), so the system was not closed.

callouts.p: Where there are energy transfers in a closed system, there is no net change to the total energy in that system.
Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but cannot be created or destroyed.

core.p: Spec 8.2 asks you to draw and interpret diagrams. Two kinds are used: **flow diagrams** (boxes for stores, arrows for transfers) and **Sankey diagrams** (arrows whose **width is proportional to the amount of energy**).
bullets: In a Sankey diagram the **input** arrow enters on the left.
**Useful** energy goes straight on; **wasted** energy usually bends downwards.
The **widths add up**: input = useful + wasted (conservation of energy).
To read values, count squares on the grid or measure widths and use the scale.
Label each arrow with the store or pathway and the amount in joules (J).
Wasted energy usually ends up in the **thermal store of the surroundings**.

callouts.p: If drawing a Sankey diagram, choose a scale (e.g. 1 square = 100 J) and make sure the output arrows together are exactly as wide as the input arrow.

core.h: Exam technique for describing energy changes
core.p: Describe questions want a clear chain: starting store, pathway, finishing store(s), and what happens to the total.
bullets: Use the pattern: 'Energy is transferred from the **___ store** of the ___ by **___ (pathway)** to the **___ store** of the ___'.
Always say **which object** owns the store (e.g. thermal store of the brakes).
Mention **wasted energy** to the thermal store of the surroundings where relevant.
For conservation questions, state that the **total energy stays the same**.
Use the unit **joule (J)** for energy.

callouts.p: Write 'transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings' or 'dissipated', never 'energy is lost' or 'used up' without saying where it went.

analogy.t: Energy as money in bank accounts
analogy.p: Think of energy stores as different bank accounts (kinetic account, thermal account, GPE account) and transfers as payments between them by different methods (card = electrically, cash = by forces, transfer = by heating). In a closed system the bank is sealed: money moves between accounts but the total never changes, exactly like conservation of energy. Wasted energy is like small fees paid into a 'surroundings' account you can't easily get back. It breaks down because energy is not a physical thing that sits somewhere like coins, and a bank can print money, whereas energy can never be created.

terms.d: An object or group of objects chosen for describing energy changes.
A system in which no energy is transferred in or out; its total energy stays constant.
A way in which energy is held by an object or system, e.g. kinetic, thermal, chemical.
Energy an object has because it is moving; more when faster or more massive.
Energy an object has because of its height in a gravitational field.
Energy stored in an object that is stretched, squashed or bent.
Energy an object has because of its temperature (the motion of its particles).
Energy stored in fuels, food and batteries, released by chemical reactions.
Energy stored in atomic nuclei, released by fission or fusion.
Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force.
Energy transferred by an electric current in a circuit.
Energy transfer from a hotter object to a cooler one because of a temperature difference.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred usefully, stored or dissipated.
Energy that is spread out to the surroundings, usually into thermal stores, and not usefully used.
An energy transfer diagram in which arrow widths are proportional to the amount of energy transferred.
The unit of energy; 1 J is the energy transferred when a force of 1 N moves 1 m.

mistakes.w: The kettle turns electrical energy into heat energy.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred electrically to the heating element and by heating to the thermal store of the water.

mistakes.w: Energy is lost when a car brakes.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the car by friction to the thermal store of the brakes and surroundings; total energy is conserved.

mistakes.w: Sound energy store / light energy store.
mistakes.r: Sound and light are ways energy is transferred, not stores.

mistakes.w: In a closed system energy stays in the same store.
mistakes.r: Energy can move between stores in a closed system; only the total energy stays the same.

mistakes.w: At the top of its flight the ball has no energy.
mistakes.r: Its kinetic store is empty but its gravitational potential store is at a maximum.

mistakes.w: Energy is used up by the motor.
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred from the chemical store of the battery, electrically, to the kinetic store of the motor and the thermal store of the surroundings.

mistakes.w: In a Sankey diagram the useful arrow is wider because it is more important.
mistakes.r: Arrow width is proportional to the amount of energy; the outputs together equal the input width.

mistakes.w: Heating means energy moves from cold to hot.
mistakes.r: By heating, energy is transferred from the hotter object to the cooler object.

exam.q: State the law of conservation of energy.
model: Energy cannot be created or destroyed (only transferred between stores).
exam.tip: Learn this exact phrasing.

exam.q: Name the energy store that increases when a spring is stretched.
model: Elastic potential (energy store).
exam.tip: Give the full name, not just 'potential'.

exam.q: State the three ways, given in the specification, in which the energy of a system can be changed.
model: Work done by forces
in electrical equipment / electrically, and in heating (both needed for second mark)
exam.tip: Two marks for three items: all three are needed for full marks.

exam.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Describe the energy transfers as the ball rises to its highest point. Ignore air resistance.
model: Energy is transferred from the kinetic (energy) store of the ball
to the gravitational potential (energy) store (by work done by the weight / gravity)
exam.tip: Name both stores and say which decreases and which increases.

exam.q: Describe the energy transfers when a car brakes to a stop.
model: Energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the car
by work done by friction (between brake pads and discs)
to the thermal store of the brakes / surroundings
exam.tip: Store, pathway, store: one mark each.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by a closed system and what happens to the total energy in a closed system.
model: No energy is transferred into or out of the system
so there is no net change to the total energy (energy just moves between stores)
exam.tip: The second mark needs 'total energy stays the same' or 'no net change'.

exam.q: An electric kettle transfers 2000 J. 1700 J is transferred to the thermal store of the water. Calculate the energy wasted and state where it goes.
model: to the thermal store of the kettle / surroundings
exam.tip: Conservation of energy: input = useful + wasted.

exam.q: Draw a Sankey diagram for a lamp that receives 100 J electrically, gives out 20 J by light and transfers 80 J to the thermal store of the surroundings.
model: Input arrow labelled 100 J
useful output labelled 20 J (light) and wasted output labelled 80 J (thermal store of surroundings) bending away
widths in proportion (wasted arrow 4 times wider than useful) and outputs add to input width
exam.tip: Use a scale, e.g. 1 square = 10 J.

exam.q: A trolley is pushed with a constant force along a level floor and speeds up. Describe the energy changes involved.
model: The force does work on the trolley
energy transferred from the chemical store of the person (muscles)
to the kinetic store of the trolley, with some to the thermal store of surroundings by friction
exam.tip: Remember where the force's energy comes from.

exam.q: A student says: 'When a falling ball hits the ground and stops, its energy has disappeared.' Explain why the student is wrong, describing the energy changes before and during the impact.
model: As the ball falls, energy is transferred from the gravitational potential store to the kinetic store
some energy transferred to thermal store of surroundings by air resistance
On impact, work is done by the contact forces deforming the ball and ground
energy transferred to the thermal stores of the ball, ground and surroundings
some transferred by sound waves (which then heats the surroundings)
energy cannot be created or destroyed, so total energy is the same; it has been dissipated, not disappeared
exam.tip: Level-marked: a logical sequence of transfers ending with conservation.

worked.q: A motor in a closed system receives 500 J electrically. It transfers 350 J to the kinetic store of a flywheel and the rest to the thermal store of the motor. How much goes to the thermal store, and what is the total energy after the transfer?
steps: Conservation of energy: energy in = sum of energy out.
The system is closed, so the total energy is unchanged.
worked.ans: 150 J to the thermal store; the total remains 500 J.

worked.q: Read a Sankey diagram drawn with a scale of 1 mm = 10 J. The input arrow is 60 mm wide, the useful arrow is 15 mm wide. Find the input energy, the useful energy and the wasted energy.
worked.ans: Input 600 J, useful 150 J, wasted 450 J.

worked.q: Model answer: describe the energy changes when water is boiled in an electric kettle.
steps: Start: energy is transferred electrically from the mains supply to the heating element.
The element heats up and energy is transferred by heating to the thermal store of the water.
The temperature of the water rises until it boils.
Some energy is wasted, transferred to the thermal store of the kettle and the surroundings, and by sound.
worked.ans: Electrical transfer to the element, then heating to the thermal store of the water (useful), with some energy dissipated to the thermal stores of the kettle and surroundings.

phy_edx.7.1.summary: Work is done when a force moves an object, and the work done is equal to the energy transferred: both are measured in joules. Work done is calculated using W = F x d, where d is the distance moved in the direction of the force, so 1 J = 1 N m. Work done by forces transfers energy between stores, for example into a kinetic or gravitational potential store, or into thermal stores when work is done against friction, and this lets you calculate energy changes in a system.

core.p: Spec points 8.5 to 8.7 are about **work done**: energy transferred when a **force moves an object**. You must describe how to **measure** the work done, know that **energy transferred (J) = work done (J)**, **recall and use W = F x d**, and **describe and calculate** the energy changes when a system is changed by work done by forces.
bullets: 8.5: describe how to measure the work done by a force; energy transferred (J) is equal to work done (J).
8.6: **recall and use** work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force.
8.7: describe and calculate the changes in energy when a system is changed by work done by forces.
The equation **W = F x d** must be **memorised**; it is a recall equation, so it is not given on the equation sheet.

callouts.p: work done (J) = force (N) x distance moved in the direction of the force (m), or W = F x d.

core.p: In physics, **work is done** whenever a **force makes an object move**. Doing work is one of the ways energy is transferred between stores (mechanically).
bullets: When work is done **on** an object, energy is transferred **to** it.
When an object does work (e.g. pushing something), energy is transferred **from** it.
No movement means **no work done**, however hard you push (e.g. pushing a wall).
Work is done by many forces: your muscles, an engine, friction, weight, magnetic and electrostatic forces.

callouts.p: Work done is the energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force. Energy transferred (J) = work done (J).

core.h: The equation W = F x d
core.p: The work done depends on two things: **how big the force is** and **how far the object moves in the direction of the force**. Double either and the work done doubles.
bullets: **W** = work done, in **joules (J)**.
**F** = force, in **newtons (N)**.
**d** = distance moved **in the direction of the force**, in **metres (m)**.
Rearranged: **F = W / d** and **d = W / F**.
Large amounts: 1 kJ = 1000 J, 1 MJ = 1 000 000 J. Convert cm to m (divide by 100) and km to m (x 1000).

head: Quantity
Symbol
Unit
rows: Distance moved in direction of force

core.h: The joule and the newton metre
core.p: Because work = force x distance, the unit of work could be written as newton metres. **One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre** in the direction of the force.
bullets: **1 J = 1 N m** (newton metre).
Lifting an apple (about 1 N) through 1 m transfers about 1 J.
Be careful: the **moment** of a force is also measured in N m, but that is a turning effect, not energy.
In energy questions always give the answer in **J**.

callouts.p: One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre in the direction of the force: 1 J = 1 N m.

core.p: Only the distance moved **in the direction of the force** counts. If a force is at **right angles** to the motion, it does **no work**.
bullets: Lifting a box: the force is upwards and the box moves upwards, so work is done.
Carrying a bag horizontally at constant height: the upward force on the bag is at **90 degrees** to the motion, so it does **no work** on the bag.
A satellite in a circular orbit: gravity acts towards the centre, at right angles to motion, so no work is done and its speed stays the same.
When lifting, the distance in the direction of the force is the **vertical height**, not the length of a slope or path.

core.p: To measure the work done by a force, you need to measure the **force** and the **distance moved in the direction of the force**, then use W = F x d.
bullets: Attach a **force meter (newtonmeter)** to a block and pull it horizontally along a bench.
Pull at a **steady speed** so the reading is steady; read the force F in N.
Measure the distance moved with a **metre rule** (or tape measure), in m.
Calculate W = F x d. This equals the energy transferred (here, to thermal stores by friction).
To measure work done lifting an object: weigh it with the force meter (weight in N), measure the vertical height in m, W = weight x height.
Repeat and take a mean to reduce the effect of random errors; read the meter at eye level.

callouts.p: At steady speed the pull equals the friction force, so the meter reading is constant and the work done all goes into overcoming friction rather than increasing kinetic energy.

core.p: Work done is a **measure of energy transferred**. Every joule of work done by a force is one joule moved from one store to another.
bullets: Pushing a trolley that speeds up: work done by you = energy transferred from your **chemical store** to the trolley's **kinetic store** (plus thermal by friction).
Lifting a box at steady speed: work done against gravity = gain in **gravitational potential store**.
Stretching a spring: work done = energy into the **elastic potential store**.
Friction doing work: energy transferred to **thermal stores** of the surfaces and surroundings (they warm up).
So you can say 'energy transferred = work done' and use the same number of joules.

callouts.p: Energy transferred (J) is equal to work done (J). If 500 J of work is done, 500 J of energy has been transferred.

core.p: Friction always opposes motion. When an object moves against friction, work is done against the friction and energy is transferred to **thermal stores**.
bullets: Rubbing your hands together: work done against friction warms them up.
Car brakes: the friction force does work on the car, transferring energy from the kinetic store to the thermal store of the brakes.
Work done against friction = friction force x distance.
This is usually **wasted (dissipated)** energy, heating the surroundings.
Air resistance is a type of friction; it does work on moving vehicles, heating the air.

core.p: Work done links forces to energy stores. You can use W = F x d to find a change in a store, or use a change in a store to find a force or distance.
bullets: Car braking: work done by brakes = kinetic energy lost, so braking force x stopping distance = initial kinetic energy.
Lifting: work done = weight x height = change in GPE (link to 8.8, GPE = m x g x h).
Constant force speeding up an object on a frictionless surface: work done = gain in kinetic energy.
If friction acts: work done by the pushing force = gain in kinetic store + energy to thermal stores.
Edexcel uses **g = 10 N/kg** on Earth; weight W = m x g.

callouts.p: If you are given a mass in kg, convert to weight in N (weight = mass x g) before using W = F x d.

core.p: If you plot force against distance moved, the **area under the graph equals the work done**. For a constant force the area is a rectangle: F x d.
bullets: Constant force: area = height x width = F x d.
This idea extends to varying forces, e.g. the area under a force-extension graph for a spring equals the energy stored.
Units of the area: N x m = J.

core.p: Edexcel calculations usually carry 2 or 3 marks: substitution, rearrangement and answer with unit.
bullets: Write the equation first: W = F x d.
**Substitute** values with units converted (cm to m, kJ to J, kg to N).
**Rearrange** before or after substituting: d = W / F, F = W / d.
Give the answer with the correct **unit** (J, N or m) and sensible significant figures.
Check: does the answer look reasonable? (Lifting a person up stairs is a few thousand joules.)

callouts.p: Even if the final answer is wrong, the substitution mark can be awarded if the working is written down.

analogy.t: Work as paying energy with a force card
analogy.p: Imagine every time a force pushes an object along, it 'pays' energy from one store into another, and the bill is force x distance. Push twice as hard, or for twice as far, and you pay twice as much. Holding a heavy bag still is like standing in the shop without buying anything: you feel tired, but no payment (work) is made on the bag because it has not moved. The analogy breaks down because there is no 'money' object being passed, and your muscles do use energy even when holding still (internally, as the muscle fibres contract), although no work is done on the bag.

terms.d: Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force.
A push or pull on an object, measured in newtons (N).

terms.t: Distance moved in the direction of the force
terms.d: The part of the object's movement along the line of the force, in metres (m).
The unit of energy and work: work done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m in the direction of the force.
Equivalent to a joule when used for work done: 1 N m = 1 J.
The unit of force.
The amount of energy moved from one store to another; equal to the work done.
An instrument, often spring based, used to measure the size of a force in newtons.
A force that opposes motion between surfaces; work done against it transfers energy to thermal stores.
The gravitational force on an object: weight = mass x gravitational field strength (W = m x g).
Force per kilogram due to gravity; 10 N/kg on Earth in Edexcel exams.
Energy held by an object because it is moving.
Energy held by an object because of its height in a gravitational field.
Energy held by an object because of its temperature.
Spreading of energy to the surroundings, usually into thermal stores, so it is less useful.

mistakes.w: Work done = force / distance.
mistakes.r: Work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force (W = F x d).

mistakes.w: Using mass in kg as the force.
mistakes.r: Convert mass to weight first: weight (N) = mass (kg) x g (10 N/kg).

mistakes.w: Using a distance in cm or km without converting.
mistakes.r: Distance must be in metres for the answer to be in joules.

mistakes.w: Holding a heavy box still does work on it.
mistakes.r: No work is done on the box because it does not move (d = 0).

mistakes.w: Using the length of a slope when finding work done against gravity.
mistakes.r: Use the vertical height, because that is the distance moved in the direction of the force (against weight).

mistakes.w: Answer given in N or W (watts).
mistakes.r: Work done and energy are measured in joules (J).

mistakes.w: Work done is the same as power.
mistakes.r: Power is the rate of doing work (work done per second); work done is the total energy transferred.

mistakes.w: Energy transferred by friction is destroyed.
mistakes.r: Work done against friction transfers energy to thermal stores; energy is conserved.

exam.q: State the equation linking work done, force and distance moved in the direction of the force.
model: work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force (W = F x d)
exam.tip: Words or symbols are both accepted; include 'in the direction of the force' if writing words.

exam.q: State the unit of work done.
model: joule / J (accept N m)
exam.tip: Not watt, not newton.

exam.q: A man pushes a car with a force of 400 N for a distance of 15 m. Calculate the work done.
exam.tip: Unit needed for full marks in many mark schemes.

exam.q: A crane does 36 000 J of work lifting a load with a force of 4500 N. Calculate the height the load is lifted.
model: d = W / F
exam.tip: Rearrangement is a separate mark: write d = W / F.

exam.q: A student pushes a box along the floor. She does 240 J of work and the box moves 80 cm. Calculate the force she uses.
exam.tip: Convert units before substituting.

exam.q: Describe how a student could measure the work done in pulling a block along a bench.
model: Attach a force meter to the block and pull it (horizontally) at a steady speed
read the force (in N) from the meter
measure the distance moved with a metre rule (in m)
calculate work done = force x distance
exam.tip: Name the equipment and say what each measures.

exam.q: A person holds a 50 N bag still for 2 minutes. Explain why no work is done on the bag.
model: The bag does not move / distance moved is zero
work done = force x distance, so W = 50 x 0 = 0
exam.tip: Link back to the equation.

exam.q: A car brakes to a stop. Describe the energy transfers and explain why the brakes get hot.
model: Energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the car
work is done by the friction force between brake pads and discs
energy is transferred to the thermal store of the brakes, so their temperature rises
exam.tip: Use the phrase 'work done by friction'.

exam.q: A cyclist applies a constant forward force of 50 N over 20 m on a level road. Friction does 300 J of work against the motion. Calculate the increase in the kinetic energy store of the cyclist.
model: Work done by cyclist = 50 x 20 = 1000 J
energy to thermal stores = 300 J
increase in kinetic store = 1000 - 300 = 700 J
exam.tip: Conservation of energy: work in = gain in KE + energy dissipated.

exam.q: A 60 kg climber climbs a 12 m vertical rock face at a steady speed. Explain how the work done is related to the energy stores of the climber, and calculate the work done against gravity (g = 10 N/kg).
model: Weight = m x g = 60 x 10 = 600 N
the distance in the direction of the force is the vertical height, 12 m
work done = F x d = 600 x 12 = 7200 J
energy transferred from the chemical store of the climber (muscles)
to the gravitational potential store of the climber (7200 J gained)
extra energy is dissipated to thermal stores of the climber / surroundings, so more than 7200 J is transferred from the chemical store
exam.tip: Show the weight calculation first, then link work done to stores.

worked.q: A box of mass 25 kg is lifted onto a shelf 1.6 m high at steady speed. Calculate the work done (g = 10 N/kg).
steps: Force needed = weight = m x g = 25 x 10 = 250 N.
Distance in the direction of the force = vertical height = 1.6 m.
worked.ans: 400 J of work is done, transferred to the gravitational potential store of the box.

worked.q: A car's brakes provide a braking force of 6000 N. The car has 150 kJ in its kinetic store. Calculate the braking distance, assuming all the kinetic energy is transferred by the brakes.
steps: Work done by brakes = kinetic energy lost = 150 000 J.

worked.q: A student pulls a block 2.5 m along a bench at steady speed. The force meter reads 4.0 N. Calculate the work done and state where the energy goes.
steps: At steady speed the kinetic store does not change, so the energy is transferred by work done against friction to the thermal stores of the block, bench and surroundings.
worked.ans: 10 J, transferred to thermal stores (the block and bench warm up slightly).

phy_edx.7.2.summary: An object raised above the ground has energy in its **gravitational potential energy store**, and the change is **change in GPE = mass x gravitational field strength x change in vertical height** (GPE = m x g x h). A moving object has energy in its **kinetic energy store**, given by **KE = 1/2 x m x v^2**. These two equations are recalled, rearranged and combined with conservation of energy, so that when an object falls with no air resistance, the GPE lost equals the KE gained (m x g x h = 1/2 x m x v^2).

core.p: When you lift an object you do work against its weight. That work is not lost: it is stored in the **gravitational potential energy store** of the object (strictly, of the object and Earth system). The higher you lift it, and the heavier it is, the more energy is stored.
bullets: Edexcel equation (recall): **change in gravitational potential energy (J) = mass (kg) x gravitational field strength (N/kg) x change in vertical height (m)**
Symbols: **delta GPE = m x g x delta h**
On Earth Edexcel uses **g = 10 N/kg** unless the question tells you otherwise
GPE depends only on the **vertical** height change, not the path taken (a ramp or a ladder to the same height gives the same GPE)
GPE is always measured from a chosen zero level, usually the ground, so we really calculate the **change** in GPE

callouts.p: change in gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength x change in vertical height

fig.cap: Lifting a mass m through a vertical height h does work against its weight (m x g), so the energy in its gravitational store increases by m x g x h. Only the vertical height counts.

core.h: Why GPE = m x g x h
core.p: This is just work done = force x distance applied to lifting. The force needed to lift an object steadily equals its **weight** (W = m x g), and the distance moved in the direction of that force is the vertical height h.
bullets: Work done lifting = force x distance = (m x g) x h
Energy transferred = work done, so this work becomes the GPE gained
That is why the unit works out: N/kg x kg = N, and N x m = **J**
Moving sideways at the same height does no work against gravity, so GPE does not change

callouts.p: The GPE gained when lifting equals the work done against gravity: m x g x h.

core.p: Most lost marks in GPE questions come from units, not physics. Convert everything to SI units before substituting.
bullets: Mass in **kilograms**: 500 g = 0.5 kg
Height in **metres**: 80 cm = 0.80 m, 2 km = 2000 m
g in **N/kg** (same as m/s^2)
Energy in **joules (J)**; 1 kJ = 1000 J, 1 MJ = 1 000 000 J
Do not confuse mass (kg) with weight (N): if you are given weight, GPE = weight x h directly

callouts.p: A 200 g ball raised 50 cm: use m = 0.2 kg and h = 0.5 m, giving 0.2 x 10 x 0.5 = 1 J, not 100 000 J.

core.h: Gravitational field strength on other planets
core.p: g is the force of gravity on each kilogram. It is different on different planets and moons, so the same object at the same height has a different GPE.
bullets: Earth: about 10 N/kg (9.8 N/kg more precisely)
Moon: about 1.6 N/kg, so lifting something 1 m on the Moon stores about one sixth of the energy it would on Earth
Mass does not change from planet to planet; weight and GPE do
Always use the g value given in the question

callouts.p: If a question says 'on Mars, g = 3.7 N/kg', use 3.7, not 10.

core.p: Any moving object has energy in its **kinetic energy store**. The faster it moves and the more mass it has, the more energy it carries.
bullets: Edexcel equation (recall): **kinetic energy (J) = 1/2 x mass (kg) x (speed (m/s))^2**
Symbols: **KE = 1/2 x m x v^2**
A stationary object has zero kinetic energy
Kinetic energy is never negative because v^2 is always positive
Direction does not matter for KE: a car at 20 m/s north has the same KE as at 20 m/s south

callouts.p: kinetic energy = 1/2 x mass x (speed)^2

core.p: Because speed is squared, KE is far more sensitive to speed than to mass. This is the heart of many 'explain' questions about road safety.
bullets: Double the mass: KE **doubles** (directly proportional to m)
Double the speed: KE is multiplied by **4** (2^2)
Triple the speed: KE x 9
Halve the speed: KE is one quarter
So a car at 60 mph has four times the KE of the same car at 30 mph, needs about four times the braking distance (same braking force), and does far more damage in a crash
A graph of KE against v is a curve (parabola); KE against v^2 is a straight line through the origin

callouts.p: In 1/2 x m x v^2 only v is squared. Work out v^2 first, then multiply by m, then halve.

fig.cap: KE against speed is a curve, not a straight line. Doubling the speed from v to 2v multiplies the kinetic energy by four, because KE is proportional to v squared.

core.p: Higher tier questions often give you the energy and ask for mass, height or speed. Rearrange before substituting, or substitute and then solve.
bullets: h = GPE / (m x g)
m = GPE / (g x h)
m = 2 x KE / v^2
v^2 = 2 x KE / m, so **v = square root of (2 x KE / m)**
Remember to take the **square root** at the end when finding speed: a very common lost mark

callouts.p: Write v^2 = ... as a separate step, then v = square root. If you forget the square root you still keep the method marks.

core.h: Energy transfers between GPE and KE
core.p: In a closed system with no friction or air resistance, energy is conserved, so energy lost from one store must appear in another. A falling object transfers energy from its gravitational store to its kinetic store; an object thrown upwards does the reverse.
bullets: Falling: GPE decreases, KE increases; the transfer is mechanical, by the work done by the object's weight
Thrown up: KE decreases, GPE increases; at the top KE is zero (vertical throw)
With no air resistance: **GPE lost = KE gained**, so m x g x h = 1/2 x m x v^2
Mass cancels: **v^2 = 2 x g x h**, so all objects dropped from the same height reach the same speed (ignoring air resistance)
Height reached by something thrown upwards at speed v: h = v^2 / (2 x g)

callouts.p: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores; in a closed system the total stays the same.

core.p: These are classic exam contexts. Track the two stores at each point and remember what friction and air resistance do.
bullets: Highest point: maximum GPE, minimum KE (zero if at rest)
Lowest point: minimum GPE, maximum KE, so maximum speed
Pendulum: GPE at the ends of the swing, KE at the bottom, swapping twice each cycle

In reality some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings by friction and air resistance, so the coaster cannot climb back to its starting height and a pendulum's swings get smaller
Then: KE gained = GPE lost - energy dissipated, so the real speed is less than the calculated ideal speed

callouts.p: Calculated speeds using mgh = 1/2mv^2 are maximum values; the real value is lower because of friction and air resistance.

core.p: Exam questions often give you the height fallen and the measured speed, then ask how much energy was dissipated. Calculate both stores separately and subtract.
bullets: Step 1: GPE lost = m x g x h
Step 2: KE gained = 1/2 x m x v^2 (using the measured speed)
Step 3: energy dissipated = GPE lost - KE gained
State where it went: to the **thermal energy store of the surroundings** (and the object) by work done against air resistance or friction
This links to efficiency: useful KE out / GPE in

callouts.p: Do both energies in J before subtracting; do not mix kJ and J.

core.p: To stop a moving vehicle, its kinetic energy must be transferred away. The brakes do work against the motion.
bullets: Work done by brakes = braking force x braking distance = KE lost
So braking distance = (1/2 x m x v^2) / braking force
Energy is transferred from the kinetic store to the **thermal store of the brakes** (they get hot) and then to the surroundings
Because KE is proportional to v^2, doubling the speed means about four times the braking distance for the same force

callouts.p: When all the KE is removed by a constant force: force x distance = 1/2 x m x v^2.

core.h: Exam technique for GPE and KE calculations
core.p: These are usually 2 or 3 mark calculations, with Higher tier versions chaining several equations together.
bullets: Write the equation in words or symbols first (often 1 mark on its own)
Convert units to kg, m, m/s
Substitute with numbers shown clearly
Give the answer with the unit (J, kg, m or m/s) and sensible significant figures
For multi-step questions, label each step (GPE lost, KE gained) so the examiner can award method marks

callouts.p: Both GPE = m x g x h and KE = 1/2 x m x v^2 must be recalled; they are not given on the Edexcel equation sheet.

analogy.t: Energy as money in two bank accounts
analogy.p: Think of GPE and KE as two bank accounts. Lifting an object deposits money into the 'height' account (GPE). As it falls, money is moved from the height account into the 'speed' account (KE). With no fees (no air resistance or friction), every pound that leaves one account arrives in the other. Air resistance is like a bank fee: some money leaks out to the thermal store of the surroundings, so the speed account gets less than the height account lost. Where it breaks down: money is a single number you can spend anywhere, but energy stores are physical properties of objects, and the 'speed account' grows with the square of speed, which no bank does.

terms.d: The energy an object has because of its position (height) in a gravitational field.
delta GPE = m x g x delta h; the energy transferred to or from the gravitational store when an object moves vertically.
The energy an object has because it is moving; KE = 1/2 x m x v^2.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg); the same everywhere.
The gravitational force on an object, W = m x g, measured in newtons (N).
The gravitational force per unit mass, in N/kg; about 10 N/kg on Earth.
The distance moved straight up or down, in metres; only the vertical change affects GPE.
Distance travelled per unit time, in m/s; squared in the KE equation.
The unit of energy; 1 J is the energy transferred when a force of 1 N moves 1 m.
Energy transferred when a force moves an object, work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred usefully, stored or dissipated; total energy in a closed system is constant.
A system where no energy enters or leaves, so the total energy does not change.
Energy transferred to stores where it is less useful, usually the thermal store of the surroundings.
A frictional force opposing motion through air; work done against it transfers energy to the thermal store of the surroundings.

mistakes.w: KE = 1/2 x (m x v)^2
mistakes.r: Only the speed is squared: KE = 1/2 x m x v^2.

mistakes.w: Using mass in grams or height in cm in the equation
mistakes.r: Convert to kg and m first, e.g. 250 g = 0.25 kg, 40 cm = 0.40 m.

mistakes.w: Finding v^2 and giving it as the speed
mistakes.r: Take the square root: v = square root of (2 x KE / m).

mistakes.w: Doubling the speed doubles the kinetic energy
mistakes.r: Doubling the speed quadruples (x4) the kinetic energy because KE is proportional to v^2.

mistakes.w: Using the distance along a slope for h
mistakes.r: Use the vertical height change only.

mistakes.w: Energy is lost when a ball falls through the air
mistakes.r: Energy is not lost; it is dissipated (transferred) to the thermal store of the surroundings by work done against air resistance.

mistakes.w: A heavier object dropped from the same height hits the ground faster (no air resistance)
mistakes.r: Mass cancels in mgh = 1/2mv^2, so all objects reach the same speed, v = square root of (2gh), ignoring air resistance.

mistakes.w: Using weight in place of mass in mgh, giving 10 times too much
mistakes.r: If given weight in N, GPE = weight x h; if given mass in kg, multiply by g.

mistakes.w: Answer given without a unit
mistakes.r: State the unit: J for energy, m/s for speed, m for height, kg for mass.

exam.q: State the equation linking change in gravitational potential energy, mass, gravitational field strength and change in vertical height.
model: change in GPE = mass x gravitational field strength x change in vertical height (delta GPE = m x g x delta h)
exam.tip: Words or standard symbols both score; do not invent your own letters.

exam.q: State the equation linking kinetic energy, mass and speed.
model: kinetic energy = 1/2 x mass x (speed)^2 (KE = 1/2 x m x v^2)
exam.tip: Make it clear only the speed is squared.

exam.q: A crate of mass 40 kg is lifted onto a lorry 1.5 m high. Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy. (g = 10 N/kg)
model: substitution: 40 x 10 x 1.5
exam.tip: Correct answer with unit scores full marks even without working, but show working in case of slips.

exam.q: A cyclist and bicycle have a total mass of 80 kg and travel at 6.0 m/s. Calculate their kinetic energy.
model: substitution: 0.5 x 80 x 6.0^2
exam.tip: Square 6.0 first (36), then x 80 x 0.5.

exam.q: A ball has 18 J of kinetic energy and a mass of 0.25 kg. Calculate its speed.
model: rearrangement: v^2 = 2 x KE / m
v = 12 m/s
exam.tip: Higher tier: don't forget the square root.

exam.q: A car's speed doubles. Explain what happens to its kinetic energy.
model: kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared
so kinetic energy increases by a factor of 4
exam.tip: Give the factor (x4), not just 'it increases'.

exam.q: A diver of mass 60 kg drops from a 10 m board. Ignoring air resistance, calculate her speed as she reaches the water. (g = 10 N/kg)
model: GPE lost = 60 x 10 x 10 = 6000 J
KE gained = GPE lost = 6000 J
exam.tip: Or use v^2 = 2gh directly, but state that GPE lost = KE gained.

exam.q: In a real dive the diver's speed is slightly less than calculated. Explain why.
model: work is done against air resistance
so some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings, so less is transferred to the kinetic store
exam.tip: Name the force and the store the energy goes to.

exam.q: A 2.0 kg rock falls 5.0 m and hits the ground at 9.0 m/s. Calculate the energy dissipated during the fall. (g = 10 N/kg)
model: GPE lost = 2.0 x 10 x 5.0 = 100 J
KE gained = 0.5 x 2.0 x 9.0^2 = 81 J
energy dissipated = 100 - 81 = 19 J
exam.tip: Calculate both stores separately then subtract.

exam.q: Describe the energy transfers for a pendulum as it swings from one side, through the lowest point, to the other side, and explain why the swings eventually stop.
model: at the highest point the bob is momentarily at rest with maximum energy in the gravitational potential store
as it falls, the gravitational store decreases and energy is transferred to the kinetic store
at the lowest point GPE is minimum and KE is maximum, so the bob is fastest
as it rises the kinetic store decreases and the gravitational store increases again
at each swing work is done against air resistance (and friction at the pivot)
so energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings, the total in the GPE/KE stores decreases and the maximum height falls until it stops
exam.tip: Use the word 'store' each time and finish with dissipation to the surroundings.

exam.q: A skier of mass 70 kg moving at 15 m/s comes to a slope. Calculate the maximum vertical height she could rise up the slope without using her poles. (g = 10 N/kg)
model: GPE gained = KE lost, so 70 x 10 x h = 7875
exam.tip: Maximum height assumes no energy dissipated; mass cancels.

worked.q: A 1200 kg car travels at 25 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy in kJ.
A 0.50 kg ball is dropped from a window 20 m above the ground. Ignoring air resistance, calculate its speed just before it hits the ground. (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: GPE lost = m x g x h = 0.50 x 10 x 20 = 100 J
No air resistance, so KE gained = GPE lost = 100 J

worked.q: A student of mass 55 kg climbs stairs with a vertical height of 4.0 m. How much energy is transferred to her gravitational store? On the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg) how much would the same climb store?
steps: Earth: delta GPE = 55 x 10 x 4.0 = 2200 J
Moon: delta GPE = 55 x 1.6 x 4.0 = 352 J
The mass is the same; only g changes
worked.ans: 2200 J on Earth; 352 J on the Moon

phy_edx.7.3.summary: In every real energy transfer some energy is **dissipated**: it spreads out into the surroundings, usually ending in the **thermal energy store of the surroundings**, where it is stored in less useful ways. Total energy is still conserved, but the dissipated energy is wasted because it can no longer easily be used. Mechanical processes are **wasteful when they cause a rise in temperature**, for example through friction, air resistance or electrical resistance, and these unwanted transfers can be reduced by lubrication, streamlining, thermal insulation and using low-resistance wires.

core.p: When energy is transferred, not all of it goes where we want it. Some is transferred to stores where it is spread out and less useful. We say this energy is **dissipated**. It is not destroyed: conservation of energy still holds.
bullets: **Dissipated** energy spreads out into the surroundings, usually as a small temperature rise in a large amount of air, ground or water
It ends up mostly in the **thermal energy store of the surroundings**
Once spread out it is very hard to collect and use again
**In all system changes** some energy is dissipated, so no real device is 100% efficient
Dissipated energy is often described as **wasted** energy

callouts.p: In all system changes, energy is dissipated, so that it is stored in less useful ways.
Energy is never lost or used up; it is transferred and dissipated. Total energy before = total energy after.

core.p: For any device we split the output into useful energy (what the device is for) and wasted energy (everything else). The two together always add up to the input.
bullets: Total energy in = useful energy out + wasted (dissipated) energy
Useful for a lamp: light; wasted: thermal energy of lamp and surroundings
Useful for a motor: kinetic energy; wasted: thermal (friction, resistance) and sound
Useful for a kettle: thermal store of the water; wasted: heating the kettle and the air, sound
Whether energy is useful depends on the purpose: for a heater, heating is useful

rows: heating by friction and resistance, sound
heating exhaust, engine and air, sound

callouts.p: Write 'thermal energy store of the surroundings', not just 'heat'.

core.h: Why dissipated energy is less useful
core.p: Useful energy is concentrated: a hot brake disc, a moving car, a charged battery. Dissipated energy is spread thinly, warming a huge amount of air by a tiny amount.
bullets: Concentrated energy can make things happen (move, light up, boil water)
Spread-out energy causes only a tiny temperature rise in the surroundings
You cannot easily use slightly warm air to do work
So the energy is still there but is 'stored in less useful ways'
Over time, energy in any system tends to spread out and become dissipated

core.h: Mechanical processes are wasteful when they cause a temperature rise
core.p: Whenever surfaces rub, or objects move through air or water, work is done against friction or drag. This raises the temperature of the parts and the surroundings, which dissipates energy by heating.
bullets: **Friction** between moving parts (axles, gears, brakes) transfers energy to the thermal store of the parts, which then heat the surroundings
**Air resistance** and **water resistance (drag)** transfer energy to the thermal store of the air or water
Work done against these forces = energy dissipated
The rise in temperature is the sign that energy is being wasted
Sound produced by machines is also wasted energy, which itself ends up warming the surroundings

callouts.p: Mechanical processes become wasteful when they cause a rise in temperature, so dissipating energy in heating the surroundings.

core.p: When a current flows through a wire with resistance, the wire heats up. Unless the device is a heater, this is wasted energy.
bullets: Electrons collide with ions in the metal lattice, making the ions vibrate more, so the temperature rises
Energy is transferred from the electrical work done to the thermal store of the wire, then the surroundings
Power cables, chargers, laptops and motors all get warm for this reason
Reducing resistance (thicker wires, low-resistance materials) reduces this waste

callouts.p: In a kettle, toaster or electric heater the heating effect is the useful output, not wasted.

core.h: Examples of dissipation in everyday systems
core.p: Exam questions often describe a situation and ask you to explain where the energy goes. Follow the energy from store to store and finish with the surroundings.
bullets: **Braking car**: kinetic store of car decreases; work done by friction in the brakes; thermal store of brakes increases; then dissipated to surroundings
**Bouncing ball**: each bounce is lower because energy is dissipated by heating the ball and floor and by sound and air resistance
**Pendulum**: swings get smaller due to air resistance and friction at the pivot
**Cyclist freewheeling** on the flat slows down: kinetic store decreases as work is done against air resistance and friction
**Phone charger**: gets warm because of resistance in its circuits

callouts.p: Answers that say 'energy goes to the brakes' miss marks; say 'thermal energy store of the brakes, then dissipated to the surroundings'.

core.p: The less friction between moving parts, the less work is done against it and the less energy is dissipated by heating.
bullets: **Lubrication** with oil or grease puts a thin layer between surfaces so they slide over each other easily
This reduces friction, so less energy is transferred to the thermal store of the parts
Ball bearings and wheels replace sliding with rolling, which reduces friction further
Smooth, well-maintained surfaces also reduce friction

fig.cap: Two ways to reduce unwanted energy transfer: a layer of oil between moving surfaces reduces friction, and an insulating layer around a hot object reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating to the surroundings.

core.p: Objects moving through air or water do work against drag. Reducing drag reduces dissipation.
bullets: **Streamlined** shapes let air flow smoothly round the object
This reduces air resistance, so less work is done against it at a given speed
Roof boxes, open windows and higher speeds all increase air resistance and wasted energy
Less energy dissipated means less fuel used for the same journey

core.p: Hot objects transfer energy to cooler surroundings by heating. Insulation reduces the **rate** of this transfer, so less energy is dissipated in a given time.
bullets: Materials with **low thermal conductivity** (such as foam, wool, fibreglass, trapped air) are good insulators
**Thicker** walls or layers of insulation reduce the rate of energy transfer
Homes: loft insulation, cavity wall insulation, double glazing, draught excluders
Lagging on hot water tanks and pipes; vacuum flasks
Lower thermal conductivity and greater thickness both mean a lower rate of energy transfer through a wall

What it reduces
How
rows: smooth air flow round the shape
gas gap between panes is a poor conductor

callouts.p: Insulation does not stop energy transfer; it slows the rate, so less energy is transferred in a given time.

core.p: Dissipation is the reason devices are not 100% efficient. The more energy is dissipated, the smaller the fraction that is useful.
bullets: Wasted energy = total input - useful output
Reducing dissipation (lubrication, insulation, streamlining) increases efficiency
No real device can reach 100% efficiency because some dissipation always happens
Efficiency calculations themselves are covered in 8.15

callouts.p: If a question gives input and useful output, the wasted energy is just the difference.

core.p: Six-mark questions reward a clear chain: starting store, how energy is transferred, where it ends up, why it is less useful, and how to reduce it.
bullets: Name the **starting store** (chemical, kinetic, electrical work)
Name the **process** (work done against friction, air resistance, current heating a resistance)
Name the **end store**: thermal energy store of the surroundings
Explain **why less useful**: spread out, small temperature rise, hard to use
Give a **reduction method** with the reason it works
Mention **conservation**: total energy stays the same

callouts.p: Link each step with 'so' or 'because' to show the reasoning chain.

analogy.t: Spilling a jug of water on a beach
analogy.p: Useful energy is like water in a jug: concentrated and easy to pour where you want. Every transfer spills some onto the sand. The spilt water is still there (energy is conserved), but it has soaked into a huge area in a thin layer, so you cannot scoop it back up and use it. Lubrication and insulation are like pouring more carefully so less is spilt. Where it breaks down: spilt water could in principle be collected, and it soaks into one place, whereas dissipated energy spreads throughout the surroundings and in practice can never be fully gathered back.

terms.d: The spreading out of energy into the surroundings so that it is stored in less useful ways.
Energy transferred to stores that are not useful for the purpose of the device, usually the thermal store of the surroundings.
Energy transferred to the store the device is designed to fill.
Energy stored in an object because of its temperature; increases when the object heats up.
Everything outside the system being studied, such as the air, ground and nearby objects.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred usefully, stored or dissipated.
A force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact; work done against it heats the surfaces.
A frictional force on an object moving through air; work done against it heats the air.
Using oil or grease between moving surfaces to reduce friction and so reduce unwanted energy transfer.
Shaping an object so air or water flows smoothly round it, reducing drag.
A material or layer that reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating.
A measure of how well a material transfers energy by conduction; low thermal conductivity means a good insulator.
An energy transfer diagram where arrow widths are proportional to the amounts of energy.
Opposition to current; causes heating of a conductor when current flows.

mistakes.w: The energy is lost / used up
mistakes.r: Energy is dissipated (transferred) to the thermal store of the surroundings; it is not lost or destroyed.

mistakes.w: Energy is turned into heat
mistakes.r: Energy is transferred by heating to the thermal energy store of the surroundings.

mistakes.w: Insulation stops heat escaping
mistakes.r: Insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating; it does not stop it.

mistakes.w: Lubrication makes the engine use less energy because oil stores energy
mistakes.r: Lubrication reduces friction, so less work is done against friction and less energy is dissipated by heating.

mistakes.w: Wasted energy disappears
mistakes.r: Wasted energy is spread out in the surroundings, stored in less useful ways.

mistakes.w: Sound is useful energy for a motor
mistakes.r: For a motor, sound is wasted energy; it is useful only for devices like loudspeakers.

mistakes.w: A ball bounces lower because it has less energy overall
mistakes.r: Total energy is conserved; some has been dissipated to the thermal store of the ball, floor and air, so less is left in its kinetic and gravitational stores.

mistakes.w: Thin walls insulate better because energy passes through quickly
mistakes.r: Thicker walls and lower thermal conductivity reduce the rate of energy transfer.

exam.q: State what is meant by energy being dissipated.
model: energy is spread out (to the surroundings) and stored in less useful ways
exam.tip: Mention 'spread out' or 'less useful' to score.

exam.q: A filament lamp gets hot when switched on. Name the store that the wasted energy ends up in.
model: thermal energy store of the surroundings
exam.tip: Just 'heat' is not enough.

exam.q: Give two ways of reducing unwanted energy transfer in a bicycle.
model: lubricate the chain / axles (with oil) to reduce friction
streamlined riding position / clothing to reduce air resistance
exam.tip: State the method and what it reduces.

exam.q: Explain why lubricating the moving parts of a machine reduces the energy wasted.
model: lubrication reduces friction between the surfaces
so less work is done against friction, so less energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the parts and surroundings
exam.tip: Link reduced friction to less heating.

exam.q: A motor is supplied with 500 J of energy. It transfers 350 J to the kinetic store of a load. Calculate the energy dissipated.
exam.tip: Conservation of energy: input = useful + wasted.

exam.q: Explain why a ball dropped onto a hard floor does not bounce back to its starting height.
model: some energy is dissipated during the fall by work done against air resistance
at the bounce some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the ball and floor and as sound
so less energy returns to the gravitational store, so it cannot reach the same height
exam.tip: Total energy is conserved; say where the missing energy went.

exam.q: Explain why the energy dissipated to the surroundings is described as less useful.
model: it is spread out over a large mass of surroundings, producing only a small temperature rise
so it is difficult to use it to do anything useful / cannot easily be transferred to useful stores
exam.tip: Use the idea of 'spread out'.

exam.q: State two factors of a house wall that affect the rate of energy transfer through it.
model: thickness of the wall
thermal conductivity of the wall material
exam.tip: Thicker and lower conductivity = slower rate.

exam.q: A car brakes to a stop. Describe the energy transfers involved.
model: energy in the kinetic store of the car decreases
work is done by friction between the brake pads and discs, increasing the thermal store of the brakes
energy is then dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings
exam.tip: Start store, process, end store.

exam.q: Describe how energy is wasted in a car engine and in a moving car, and explain ways these unwanted energy transfers can be reduced.
model: fuel's chemical store transfers energy, but much goes to the thermal store of the engine and exhaust gases
friction between moving parts in the engine and wheels raises their temperature, dissipating energy to the surroundings
work done against air resistance transfers energy to the thermal store of the air
sound is produced, which is also wasted and ends up heating the surroundings
lubricating moving parts with oil reduces friction so less energy is dissipated by heating
a streamlined body shape (and removing roof racks) reduces air resistance, so less work done against drag and less fuel used
exam.tip: Cover both where energy is wasted and a reason for each reduction method.

worked.q: A kettle is supplied with 240 000 J. The water gains 204 000 J. How much energy is wasted, and where does it go?
steps: Conservation of energy: total in = useful + wasted
It goes to the thermal store of the kettle body and the air around it (and a little as sound), then is dissipated to the surroundings
worked.ans: 36 000 J, dissipated to the thermal store of the kettle and surroundings

worked.q: A crate of mass 20 kg slides down a ramp. It loses 400 J from its gravitational store and gains 250 J in its kinetic store. Explain what happened to the rest of the energy and suggest one way to reduce it.
steps: Work was done against friction between the crate and the ramp (and against air resistance)
This raised the temperature of the crate and ramp, transferring 150 J to their thermal stores and then to the surroundings
Reduce it by lubricating the ramp or using rollers, which reduce friction
worked.ans: 150 J dissipated by friction to thermal stores; reduce by lubrication or rollers

worked.q: Explain why fitting loft insulation reduces a family's heating bills.
steps: Energy is transferred by heating from the warm house to the colder air outside through the roof
Loft insulation has a low thermal conductivity (it traps air) and adds thickness
This reduces the rate of energy transfer through the roof
So less energy is dissipated to the surroundings each hour, the heating needs to supply less energy, and bills fall
worked.ans: Insulation lowers the rate of energy transfer through the roof, so less energy must be supplied

phy_edx.7.4.summary: **Power** is the **rate at which energy is transferred** (or the rate at which work is done): it tells you how quickly, not how much. Edexcel students must recall and use **power (W) = work done (J) / time taken (s)**, written P = E / t, and recall that **one watt is equal to one joule per second (1 W = 1 J/s)**. Two devices can transfer the same energy, but the one that does it in less time has the greater power.

core.p: Power is not the same as energy. Energy is how much is transferred; power is how fast it is transferred. A powerful motor lifts a load quickly; a less powerful one can lift the same load to the same height, but takes longer.
bullets: **Power is the rate at which energy is transferred**
Equivalently, power is the rate at which work is done
'Rate' means 'per second'
More power = more energy transferred every second
Same energy in less time = more power

callouts.p: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred (or the rate at which work is done).

fig.cap: Two motors lift the same load through the same height, so each does 600 J of work. Motor B does it in half the time, so its power is twice as large.

core.p: Edexcel requires you to recall and use this equation. It works for any energy transfer, whether by a force doing work, by an electric current or by heating.
bullets: **power (W) = work done (J) / time taken (s)**
Symbols: **P = E / t** (E = energy transferred or work done)
Rearranged: **E = P x t** and **t = E / P**
Work done and energy transferred are the same thing, so either word can appear

callouts.p: P = E / t must be recalled; it is not on the equation sheet.

core.p: The SI unit of power is the **watt (W)**. It is defined directly from the equation: one joule transferred every second.
bullets: **1 watt = 1 joule per second (1 W = 1 J/s)**
A 60 W lamp transfers 60 J of energy every second
A 2 kW kettle transfers 2000 J every second
The watt is named after James Watt
Do not confuse the symbol W for watt with W sometimes used for work done or weight

callouts.p: One watt is equal to one joule per second (J/s).

fig.cap: Power ratings tell you how many joules each device transfers per second: 10 W means 10 J every second, 2 kW means 2000 J every second (bars not to scale).
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#1b2540"/></marker></defs><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="370" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="60" y2="30" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="14" y="24" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">energy per second (J)</text><rect x="90" y="160" width="50" height="40" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1d4ed8"/><text x="84" y="218" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">LED 10 W</text><rect x="180" y="120" width="50" height="80" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#92400e"/><text x="166" y="218" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">TV 100 W</text><rect x="270" y="50" width="50" height="150" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#b91c1c"/><text x="252" y="218" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">kettle 2 kW</text><text x="80" y="152" font-size="11" fill="#1d4ed8">10 J/s</text><text x="174" y="112" font-size="11" fill="#92400e">100 J/s</text><text x="262" y="42" font-size="11" fill="#b91c1c">2000 J/s</text><text x="330" y="120" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">not to</text><text x="330" y="136" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">scale</text></svg>

core.p: Power and time are often given in awkward units. Convert to watts and seconds before using P = E / t.
bullets: 1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W
1 megawatt (MW) = 1 000 000 W
1 minute = 60 s; 1 hour = 3600 s
Example: 3 minutes = 180 s; 1.5 kW = 1500 W

callouts.p: The most common slip: using minutes instead of seconds. 2 minutes is 120 s.

core.p: The spec asks you to use examples to explain the definition. The best examples compare two situations that transfer the same energy at different rates, or the same time with different energies.
bullets: Two cranes lift identical loads to the same height: same work done, but the one that takes less time is more powerful
Running up stairs vs walking up: same gain in GPE, but running takes less time, so your power is greater
A 2 kW kettle boils water faster than a 1 kW kettle: it transfers energy to the water at twice the rate
Two lamps: a 100 W lamp transfers twice as much energy every second as a 50 W lamp
A car with a more powerful engine can accelerate faster because it can transfer energy to its kinetic store more quickly

callouts.p: When explaining, keep one quantity the same (energy or time) and show how the other changes power.

core.h: Power when a force does work
core.p: When a force moves an object, power links to work done: P = work done / time = (F x d) / t.
bullets: Work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force
Then power = work done / time
For lifting: work done = weight x height = m x g x h, so P = m x g x h / t
Higher tier link: since d / t = speed, P = F x v for a constant force at constant speed (useful but not required to recall)

callouts.p: Many 3-4 mark questions need W = F x d first, then P = W / t.

core.p: If you plot energy transferred against time, the gradient tells you the power.
bullets: Straight line through the origin: constant power
Steeper line: greater power (more joules per second)
Gradient = change in energy / change in time = power
A curve would show the power changing

fig.cap: Energy transferred against time for two devices. The gradient is energy per second, which is the power, so the steeper red line shows the more powerful device.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><defs><marker id="ah" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#1b2540"/></marker></defs><rect x="0" y="0" width="400" height="240" fill="#f8fafc"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="370" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="60" y2="20" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="300" y="222" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">time (s)</text><text x="68" y="24" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">energy (J)</text><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="230" y2="40" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="350" y2="130" stroke="#1d4ed8" stroke-width="3"/><text x="200" y="74" font-size="12" fill="#b91c1c">steep: high power</text><text x="250" y="124" font-size="12" fill="#1d4ed8">shallow: low power</text><rect x="120" y="156" width="170" height="24" rx="5" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#6b21a8"/><text x="130" y="173" font-size="12" fill="#6b21a8">gradient = power</text></svg>

core.p: A common class activity (not a core practical) is measuring how powerful you are when climbing stairs. It combines GPE and power.
bullets: Measure your mass m with bathroom scales (kg)
Measure the vertical height h of the stairs with a metre rule or tape measure (count steps x height of one step)
Time how long it takes to run up, t, with a stopwatch
Work done = gain in GPE = m x g x h
Power = m x g x h / t
Repeat and take a mean to reduce the effect of random errors in timing
Only the vertical height matters, not the length of the staircase

callouts.p: Use dry stairs, sensible footwear and a handrail; do not run if unsafe.

fig.cap: Measuring personal power: the work done climbing the stairs is the gain in GPE (m x g x h), and dividing by the time taken gives the power developed.
