core.p: Electrical appliances have a power rating showing the rate at which they transfer energy from the mains or a battery. P = E / t applies just the same.
bullets: Energy transferred by an appliance = power x time (E = P x t)
A 1500 W hair dryer on for 120 s transfers 1500 x 120 = 180 000 J
Higher power appliances transfer more energy in the same time, so cost more to run for that time
Power ratings do not tell you how efficient a device is, only how fast it transfers energy

callouts.p: Use this whenever you know the power and want the energy transferred in a given time.

core.p: Not all of the input power ends up as useful output power; some is dissipated. That is why devices quote an input power and why efficiency can also be calculated using powers.
bullets: Total input power = useful output power + wasted power
A 60 W lamp transferring 6 J/s as light wastes 54 J/s by heating
Efficiency with powers is covered in 8.15

core.p: Power questions are usually 2 or 3 marks; Higher tier ones chain equations together or need rearranging.
bullets: Write P = E / t first
Convert kW to W, kJ to J, minutes to seconds
Substitute clearly, then calculate
Give the unit: W (or J/s), J or s
In explain questions use 'rate', 'per second' and compare energy and time

callouts.p: Writing 'J/s' or 'W' for power is fine; writing 'J' for power is wrong.

analogy.t: Filling a bath with different taps
analogy.p: Energy is like the water in a bath; power is how fast the tap fills it (litres per second). A big tap (high power) and a small tap (low power) can both fill the bath completely, but the big tap does it in less time. One watt is like a tap delivering one litre every second: one joule every second. Where it breaks down: the water stays in the bath, but in real devices some energy is dissipated to the surroundings along the way, and energy can be transferred in many different ways, not just one flow.

terms.d: The rate at which energy is transferred, or the rate at which work is done.
The unit of power; 1 W = 1 joule per second (J/s).
1000 watts.
The amount of energy moved from one store to another, in joules (J).
Energy transferred when a force moves an object; work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force.
The unit of energy and work done; 1 J = 1 N x 1 m.
How quickly something happens, i.e. amount per unit time.
The duration of the energy transfer, measured in seconds (s).
The power of an appliance, showing how many joules it transfers per second when working normally.
Change in energy divided by change in time; equal to the power.
Energy stored due to height; gain in GPE = m x g x h, used to find power when lifting.
The power a person develops, e.g. m x g x h / t when climbing stairs.

mistakes.w: Power is the amount of energy a device uses
mistakes.r: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred (energy per second).

mistakes.w: Using time in minutes in P = E / t
mistakes.r: Convert time to seconds first, e.g. 5 min = 300 s.

mistakes.w: 1 watt = 1 joule
mistakes.r: 1 watt = 1 joule per second (J/s).

mistakes.w: Using 2 kW as 2 in the equation
mistakes.r: Convert to watts: 2 kW = 2000 W.

mistakes.w: P = E x t
mistakes.r: P = E / t; E = P x t is the rearrangement for energy.

mistakes.w: A more powerful motor does more work lifting the same load to the same height
mistakes.r: It does the same work, but in less time.

mistakes.w: Giving the unit of power as J
mistakes.r: Power is in W (or J/s).

mistakes.w: Using the length of the staircase for h when finding personal power
mistakes.r: Use the vertical height of the stairs.

exam.q: State what is meant by power.
model: the rate at which energy is transferred / the rate of doing work
exam.tip: The word 'rate' (or 'per second') is essential.

exam.q: State the equation linking power, work done and time taken.
model: power = work done / time taken (P = E / t)
exam.tip: Recall equation, not on the sheet.

exam.q: Which of these is equal to 1 watt? A 1 J x s  B 1 J/s  C 1 N/m  D 1 N x s
model: B (1 J/s)
exam.tip: Watt = joule per second.

exam.q: A motor does 4800 J of work in 12 s. Calculate its power.
exam.tip: Unit required for full marks.

exam.q: A 2.5 kW kettle is switched on for 3 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred.
model: convert: 2500 W and 180 s
exam.tip: Two conversions before you start.

exam.q: A 60 W lamp transfers 9000 J. Calculate how long it was switched on.
exam.tip: Rearrange first.

exam.q: Two students of equal mass climb the same stairs. Student A takes 5 s and student B takes 8 s. Explain which student develops the greater power.
model: both do the same work / gain the same GPE (same mass, same height)
A takes less time, so A transfers energy at a greater rate / has greater power
exam.tip: Same energy, less time = more power.

exam.q: A crane lifts a 500 kg load through a vertical height of 12 m in 20 s. Calculate the power output of the crane. (g = 10 N/kg)
model: work done = m x g x h = 500 x 10 x 12 = 60 000 J
exam.tip: Two equations chained together.

exam.q: A student pushes a box with a force of 150 N for 8.0 m in 30 s. Calculate the power.
model: work done = 150 x 8.0 = 1200 J
exam.tip: W = F x d first.

exam.q: Describe how a student could find her personal power by running up a flight of stairs. Include the measurements she should take and how she would calculate the power.
model: measure her mass using bathroom scales (in kg)
measure the vertical height of the stairs with a metre rule / tape measure (e.g. height of one step x number of steps)
time how long she takes to run up the stairs using a stopwatch
calculate work done / gain in GPE = mass x g x height
calculate power = work done / time taken
repeat several times and calculate a mean time to reduce random error
exam.tip: Each measurement needs the instrument; finish with both equations.

exam.q: Explain, using an example, why a 3 kW electric heater warms a room faster than a 1 kW heater.
model: 3 kW heater transfers 3000 J per second, the 1 kW heater 1000 J per second
so it transfers the energy needed in a third of the time / transfers energy at a greater rate
exam.tip: Turn kW into J per second to show understanding.

worked.q: An electric motor lifts a 40 kg load through 3.0 m in 6.0 s. Calculate the useful power output. (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: Work done = gain in GPE = m x g x h

worked.q: A 1.2 kW microwave cooks food for 2 minutes 30 seconds. How much energy is transferred, in kJ?
A 65 kg student runs up stairs of vertical height 3.6 m. Her power is 520 W. How long does she take? (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: Work done = m x g x h = 65 x 10 x 3.6 = 2340 J

phy_edx.7.5.summary: Efficiency tells you what fraction of the energy supplied to a device ends up in the store you actually want. Edexcel 1PH0 expects you to recall and use efficiency = (useful energy transferred by the device) / (total energy supplied to the device), give the answer as a decimal or a percentage, and explain why no real device can be 100% efficient because some energy is always dissipated, usually heating the surroundings. You must also explain how efficiency can be improved, for example by lubrication or thermal insulation, and apply the same idea using power instead of energy.

core.p: Whenever a device transfers energy, only part of it goes into the **useful** store. The rest is **wasted**, usually **dissipated** to the thermal store of the surroundings. Efficiency measures how good a device is at turning the energy supplied into useful output.
bullets: **Useful energy**: energy transferred to the store you want (e.g. kinetic store of a car, light from a lamp).
**Wasted energy**: energy transferred to stores you do not want, usually thermal energy of the device and surroundings, and sound.
By **conservation of energy**, total energy supplied = useful energy + wasted energy.
A more efficient device wastes a **smaller fraction** of the energy supplied.
Efficiency has **no unit**: it is a ratio of two energies, so the joules cancel.

callouts.p: efficiency = useful energy transferred by the device / total energy supplied to the device

core.p: This is a **recall** equation on Edexcel papers: it is not on the equation sheet, so learn it word for word. Both energies must be in the same unit (usually joules).
bullets: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input.
Multiply by 100 to give a **percentage**: percentage efficiency = (useful / total) x 100%.
A decimal answer is always between **0 and 1**; a percentage between **0% and 100%**.
Rearranged: useful energy = efficiency x total energy supplied.
Rearranged: total energy supplied = useful energy / efficiency.
If the question gives a percentage, convert to a decimal (divide by 100) before using it in a rearranged equation.

callouts.p: Either form scores the mark if correct, but never write 25 with no % sign or 0.25%. Give the form the question asks for.

core.p: Power is the rate of energy transfer (P = E / t). If useful and total energy are measured over the **same time**, the time cancels, so efficiency can be worked out from powers as well.
bullets: efficiency = useful power output / total power input.
Example: a 60 W motor that gives 45 W of useful mechanical power has efficiency 45 / 60 = 0.75 (75%).
Wasted power = total power - useful power, here 15 W.
Power in **watts (W)**, energy in **joules (J)**: 1 W = 1 J/s.
If one value is given as energy and the other as power, use E = P x t to convert first.

callouts.p: You can only use powers in place of energies because both are measured over the same time, so the t cancels in the ratio.

core.p: A Sankey diagram shows energy transfers with arrows whose **width is proportional to the amount of energy**. The useful arrow goes straight on and the wasted arrow bends away (usually downwards).
bullets: Width of input arrow = total energy supplied.
Widths of the output arrows **add up** to the input width (conservation of energy).
Efficiency = width of useful arrow / width of input arrow.
If drawn on squared paper, count squares: e.g. 10 squares wide in, 4 squares useful, efficiency 0.4.
The wider the wasted arrow, the less efficient the device.

core.p: In every real mechanical or electrical process, some energy is **dissipated**: it spreads out into the surroundings and becomes less useful. This is why efficiency is always less than 1.
bullets: **Friction** between moving parts heats them up, transferring energy to the thermal store.
**Air resistance (drag)** does work against moving objects, heating the air.
**Electrical resistance**: a current in wires heats them (energy transferred to the thermal store).
**Sound** is produced by vibrating parts, which eventually heats the surroundings.
The dissipated energy is still there (energy is conserved) but it is spread out and **cannot easily be used**.
Efficiency greater than 1 (or 100%) would mean creating energy, which breaks the conservation of energy.

callouts.t: Energy is not lost or destroyed
callouts.p: Do not write that energy is 'lost' or 'used up'. Write that it is **dissipated** or **transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings**.

core.h: Mechanical example: a motor lifting a load
core.p: An electric motor lifting a load is a classic Edexcel context. The useful energy is the gain in gravitational potential energy of the load; the total energy is the electrical energy supplied.
bullets: Useful energy = gain in GPE = m x g x h (g = 10 N/kg on Edexcel papers).
Total energy supplied = electrical energy, often found from E = P x t.
Wasted energy: heating of the motor coils (resistance), friction in the bearings, sound.
Efficiency = mgh / (P x t).
If the load also speeds up, its gain in kinetic energy (1/2 m v^2) is useful too.

core.p: In 'state the useful energy' questions, name the store or transfer the device is designed for.
bullets: Identify the purpose of the device first: what is it for?
Anything not linked to that purpose is wasted.
Heat is wasted in most devices, except heaters and kettles where heating IS the useful output.

callouts.p: An electric heater is close to 100% efficient because almost all the electrical energy ends up heating the room, which is what it is for.

core.p: To make a device more efficient you reduce the energy that is wasted, so a larger fraction of the energy supplied is useful.
bullets: **Lubrication** (oil, grease) reduces friction between moving surfaces, so less energy heats them.
**Thermal insulation** reduces unwanted energy transfer by heating, e.g. lagging a hot water tank or insulating a kettle.
**Streamlining** reduces air resistance on vehicles.
Using wires with **low resistance** (thicker or better conductors) reduces heating in circuits.
**Tightening loose parts** reduces vibration and sound.
Using better technology, e.g. LED lamps instead of filament lamps, wastes far less energy as heat.

core.p: Insulation improves efficiency of heating systems by slowing down energy transfer to the surroundings.
bullets: Materials with **lower thermal conductivity** transfer energy more slowly by conduction.
**Thicker** insulation gives a slower rate of energy transfer.
Cavity wall insulation, loft insulation and double glazing reduce the rate of energy loss from homes.
Less energy wasted means less fuel or electricity needs to be supplied for the same useful heating.

callouts.p: Insulation reduces the **rate** of energy transfer; it does not stop it completely.

core.p: Exam questions often give data on two devices and ask which is better. Efficiency is one factor, but cost, lifetime and power output matter too.
bullets: A higher efficiency means **less energy wasted** for the same useful output.
So less energy needs to be supplied, meaning **lower running costs** and less fuel burned.
Burning less fossil fuel in power stations means **less carbon dioxide** emitted.
Compare using numbers: calculate efficiency for each device before concluding.
Consider other factors: purchase price, lifetime, useful power output.

callouts.p: In compare questions, quote calculated efficiencies from both devices; a statement with no numbers rarely gets full marks.

core.p: Follow the same layout every time so you pick up method marks even if you slip on arithmetic.
bullets: Write the equation in words or symbols.
Substitute values with units, both in the same unit (convert kJ to J if needed: 1 kJ = 1000 J).
Calculate, then state the answer as a decimal or percentage.
Check: is your answer less than 1 (or 100%)? If not, you divided the wrong way round.
Wasted energy questions: wasted = total - useful.

callouts.p: If you get an efficiency over 1, you have done total / useful. Swap them.

analogy.p: Think of the energy supplied as water poured into a watering can, and the useful energy as the water that actually reaches the plants. Holes in the can (friction, resistance, sound) let some water drip onto the path. Efficiency is the fraction of water that reached the plants. Patching holes (lubrication, insulation) raises efficiency, and you can never get more water out than you put in. Where it breaks down: spilt water can be mopped up and reused, but dissipated energy spreads out so thinly into the surroundings that it is practically impossible to collect and use again.

terms.d: The ratio of useful energy transferred by a device to the total energy supplied to the device; no unit.
Energy transferred to the store that the device is designed to fill.
Energy transferred to stores that are not wanted, usually the thermal store of the surroundings.
All the energy put into a device, equal to useful plus wasted energy.
The spreading out of energy into the surroundings so it becomes less useful.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores or dissipated.
Efficiency multiplied by 100%.
The rate of energy transfer, P = E / t, measured in watts.
The unit of power; 1 W is a transfer of 1 joule per second.
The unit of energy.
A diagram of energy transfers in which arrow width is proportional to the energy transferred.
Using oil or grease between surfaces to reduce friction and so reduce energy wasted by heating.
Material that reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating.
A measure of how quickly a material transfers energy by conduction; lower conductivity means better insulation.
A force opposing motion between surfaces that causes energy to be transferred to the thermal store.

mistakes.w: Efficiency = total energy / useful energy
mistakes.r: efficiency = useful energy transferred / total energy supplied (answer must be less than 1)

mistakes.w: Energy is lost as heat
mistakes.r: Energy is dissipated / transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings

mistakes.w: Efficiency = 0.35%
mistakes.r: Efficiency = 0.35 or 35%, not a mix of both

mistakes.w: Efficiency measured in joules
mistakes.r: Efficiency has no unit

mistakes.w: Efficiency of 120%
mistakes.r: Efficiency can never exceed 100% because energy cannot be created

mistakes.w: Lubrication removes friction
mistakes.r: Lubrication reduces friction, so less energy is wasted heating the moving parts

mistakes.w: Using 2 kJ and 500 J directly: 500/2 = 250
mistakes.r: Convert to the same unit first: 500 / 2000 = 0.25

mistakes.w: The efficient motor uses less energy
mistakes.r: The more efficient motor wastes a smaller fraction of the energy supplied, so less input is needed for the same useful output

mistakes.w: Wasted energy = useful energy / total
mistakes.r: Wasted energy = total energy supplied - useful energy transferred

exam.q: State the equation linking efficiency, useful energy transferred and total energy supplied.
model: efficiency = useful energy transferred by the device / total energy supplied to the device
exam.tip: This is a recall equation; it is not on the equation sheet.

exam.q: A lamp is supplied with 200 J of energy and transfers 30 J as light. Calculate its efficiency.
model: Substitution: 30 / 200
exam.tip: Show the substitution for the first mark.

exam.q: A kettle has an efficiency of 0.90. It is supplied with 240 000 J. Calculate the useful energy transferred to the water.
model: useful energy = 0.90 x 240 000
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: Explain why the efficiency of a motor can never be 100%.
model: Some energy is always transferred to the thermal store / dissipated (e.g. by friction or resistance in the coils)
so useful energy output is always less than the total energy supplied
exam.tip: Name a cause and link it to a smaller useful output.

exam.q: A motor is supplied with 500 J and has an efficiency of 60%. Calculate the energy wasted.
model: useful = 0.60 x 500 = 300 J
wasted = 500 - 300
exam.tip: Or wasted = 0.40 x 500 directly.

exam.q: Describe one way of improving the efficiency of a machine with moving parts.
model: Lubricate the moving parts / use oil
reduces friction so less energy is wasted heating the parts
exam.tip: Give the method AND how it reduces wasted energy.

exam.q: An electric motor has an input power of 80 W and a useful output power of 52 W. Calculate its percentage efficiency.
exam.tip: Powers can be used in place of energies.

exam.q: A motor supplied with 1500 J lifts a 5.0 kg mass through 6.0 m. Calculate the efficiency. (g = 10 N/kg)
model: GPE = m x g x h = 5.0 x 10 x 6.0
efficiency = 300 / 1500
exam.tip: Useful energy here is the gain in GPE.

exam.q: Energy supplied to a light bulb is 60 J each second. Its efficiency is 0.25. Calculate the total energy supplied to produce 900 J of light.
model: total = useful / efficiency
exam.tip: The 60 J per second is extra information here.

exam.q: A family is choosing between two washing machines. Machine A is supplied with 2.0 kJ per wash and transfers 1.4 kJ usefully. Machine B has an efficiency of 0.62. Explain which machine is better and the benefits of choosing it.
model: Efficiency of A = 1.4 / 2.0 = 0.70 (70%)
B is 0.62 (62%), so A is more efficient
A wastes a smaller fraction of energy supplied
so less energy needs to be supplied for the same useful output
lower electricity bills / running costs
less fuel burned in power stations so less CO2 / pollution
but other factors such as purchase price or lifetime may also matter
exam.tip: Level-marked: calculate, compare, then give consequences linked together.

worked.q: An electric motor is supplied with 2.4 kJ of energy and lifts a 12 kg box through 1.5 m. Calculate the efficiency of the motor as a percentage. (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: Useful energy = gain in GPE = m x g x h = 12 x 10 x 1.5 = 180 J

worked.q: An LED lamp has an efficiency of 40%. It transfers 18 J of light energy every second. Calculate the input power of the lamp and the power wasted.
steps: Useful power = 18 J per second = 18 W
worked.ans: Input power 45 W; wasted power 27 W

worked.q: A car engine transfers 3.0 MJ of chemical energy from fuel. 0.75 MJ ends up in the kinetic store of the car. Find the efficiency and suggest why it is so low.
steps: Units cancel since both are in MJ
Most energy (2.25 MJ) is dissipated heating the engine, exhaust gases and surroundings
Friction between moving parts and air resistance also waste energy
worked.ans: 0.25 (25%); most energy is dissipated as heating due to friction and hot exhaust gases
